slides.lead: Your baby can hear sounds you can't. For a few more months.
slides.sub: Between 6 and 12 months the ear stops tracking differences its language never uses.

figure.label: babies at 6 to 8 months heard a contrast most adults cannot

slides.head: The setup
slides.body:
In 1984, Janet Werker and Richard Tees played English-learning babies two consonants from Thompson, a Salish language of British Columbia.

The sounds differ only in where the back of the tongue blocks the air. English uses one of them, so English-speaking adults hear them as the same sound.

slides.head: Who could tell them apart
slides.body: Same test, same sounds, four months apart. Nothing was wrong with their ears.

slides.head: The catch
slides.body:
Small groups, one lab, one contrast. And it is about experience, not age: babies raised in Hindi- or Thompson-speaking homes still heard their own contrasts easily at 11 to 12 months.

The window is not a wall, either. It narrows; it does not slam.

slides.head: The part that matters at home
slides.body:
Kuhl, Tsao and Liu later gave 9-month-olds twelve short sessions with live Mandarin speakers. Those babies kept hearing Mandarin contrasts.

Babies given the same material on video or audio alone learned nothing from it. A person in the room did what a screen could not.
